A curated list of readings behind CRASR's [AI-use policy](https://github.com/CRASR/ai-use) and [how we use AI](../ai.qmd). It is not a systematic review. Each entry has a one-line note on what kind of evidence it is and why it is here. Preprints and blog posts are marked; they have not been peer reviewed.

Download the full list: [RIS](resources/ai-science-reading-list.ris) (Zotero, EndNote, Mendeley) · [BibTeX](resources/ai-science-reading-list.bib)

## Incentives and the science of science

- Bergstrom, Carl T. & West, Jevin D. (2023). How publishers can fight misinformation in and about science and medicine. *Nature Medicine*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-023-02411-7)  
  Commentary anticipating generative AI flooding review and raising verification burdens.
- Gartenberg, Claudine; Hasan, Sharique; Murray, Alex & Pierce, Lamar (2026). More versus better: Artificial intelligence, incentives, and the emerging crisis in peer review. *Organization Science*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2026.ed.v37.n3)  
  Editorial with journal-level data: AI-era submissions rose while writing quality fell, adding review burden without matching gains.
- Hao, Qianyue; Xu, Fengli; Li, Yong & Evans, James (2026). Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus. *Nature* 649: 1237-1243. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09922-y)  
  Bibliometric study of 41 million papers: AI use tracks with individual career gains and a narrower collective scientific focus.
- Ioannidis, John P. A. (2005). Why most published research findings are false. *PLOS Medicine* 2(8): e124. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124)  
  Formal analysis of how power, bias, and selection shape the reliability of published findings.
- Munafò, Marcus R., et al. (2017). A manifesto for reproducible science. *Nature Human Behaviour* 1: 0021. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-016-0021)  
  Practices, incentives, and institutional reform for reproducibility; better tools need better incentives.
- Noy, Shakked & Zhang, Whitney (2023). Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence. *Science* 381: 187-192. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adh2586)  
  Randomized experiment: time and quality gains on professional writing tasks. A counterweight to a pure speed-versus-quality story.
- Smaldino, Paul E. & McElreath, Richard (2016). The natural selection of bad science. *Royal Society Open Science* 3: 160384. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.160384)  
  Formal model: rewarding publication counts selects for weak methods without anyone intending misconduct.
- Wang, Hanchen, et al. (2023). Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence. *Nature* 620: 47-60. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06221-2)  
  Review of AI's contributions across scientific discovery, broader than language-model assistants.
- West, Jevin D. & Bergstrom, Carl T. (2021). Misinformation in and about science. *PNAS* 118(15): e1912444117. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1912444117)  
  Synthesis linking misinformation within science to incentives and publishing practice. See the 2024 correction.

## Understanding, judgment, and learning

- Amano, Tatsuya; Ramírez-Castañeda, Valeria; Berdejo-Espinola, Violeta, et al. (2023). The manifold costs of being a non-native English speaker in science. *PLOS Biology* 21(7): e3002184. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3002184)  
  Survey of environmental scientists: non-native English speakers spend up to twice as long reading and writing papers.
- Bastani, Hamsa; Bastani, Osbert; Sungu, Alp; Ge, Haosen; Kabakcı, Özge & Mariman, Rei (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. *PNAS* 122: e2422633122. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122)  
  Field experiment separating assisted performance from learning; tutor design matters.
- Berdejo-Espinola, Violeta & Amano, Tatsuya (2023). AI tools can improve equity in science. *Science* 379: 991. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adg9714)  
  Letter arguing AI translation and editing can reduce language barriers in science.
- Emig, Janet (1977). Writing as a mode of learning. *College Composition and Communication* 28(2): 122-128. [Link](https://doi.org/10.58680/ccc197716382)  
  Foundational argument that writing is a way of learning, not only of reporting finished ideas.
- Goddard, Kate; Roudsari, Abdul & Wyatt, Jeremy C. (2012). Automation bias: A systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators. *Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association* 19(1): 121-127. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1136/amiajnl-2011-000089)  
  Systematic review of over-reliance on automated recommendations; predates language models.
- Graham, Steve; Kiuhara, Sharlene A. & MacKay, Meade (2020). The effects of writing on learning in science, social studies, and mathematics: A meta-analysis. *Review of Educational Research* 90(2): 179-226. [Link](https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320914744)  
  Meta-analysis: writing supports learning in school settings.
- Kazemitabaar, M.; Ye, R.; Wang, X.; Henley, A. Z.; Denny, P.; Craig, M. & Grossman, T. (2024). CodeAid: Evaluating a classroom deployment of an LLM-based programming assistant that balances student and educator needs. *Proceedings of the 2024 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642773)  
  A semester-long classroom deployment of an assistant built to explain rather than hand over code.
- Kosmyna, Nataliya; Hauptmann, Eugene; Yuan, Ye Tong; Situ, Jessica; Liao, Xian-Hao; Beresnitzky, Ashly Vivian; Braunstein, Iris & Maes, Pattie (2025). Your brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of cognitive debt when using an AI assistant for essay writing task. *arXiv:2506.08872*. [Preprint] [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2506.08872)  
  EEG study: essay writers using an AI assistant showed weaker brain connectivity, lower ownership, and poorer recall of their own text.
- Lee, Hao-Ping, et al. (2025). The impact of generative AI on critical thinking: Self-reported reductions in cognitive effort and confidence effects from a survey of knowledge workers. *Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713778)  
  Survey: more confidence in AI went with less reported critical thinking (self-report, not causal).
- Messeri, Lisa & Crockett, M. J. (2024). Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research. *Nature* 627: 49-58. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07146-0)  
  Conceptual account of how AI can raise output while narrowing understanding and intellectual diversity.
- Nature Reviews Bioengineering (2025). Writing is thinking. *Nature Reviews Bioengineering* 3: 431. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44222-025-00323-4)  
  Editorial on the value of human-generated scientific writing in the age of language models.
- Sharma, Mrinank, et al. (2024). Towards understanding sycophancy in language models. *International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024)*. [Link](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/0105f7972202c1d4fb817da9f21a9663-Abstract-Conference.html)  
  Experiments showing assistants tend to agree with users even against the truth; AI approval is not independent criticism.
- Shen, J. H. & Tamkin, A. (2026). How AI impacts skill formation. *arXiv:2601.20245*. [Preprint] [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2601.20245)  
  Randomized trial: developers who delegated a new task to AI learned it less well than those who asked conceptual questions.
- Çetinkaya-Rundel, Mine (2026). Beyond the prompt: Programming as a pathway to statistical thinking. *Talk, R+AI Conference*. [Link](https://github.com/mine-cetinkaya-rundel/beyond-the-prompt-rai-2026/blob/main/examples/hw/AGENTS.md)  
  Talk and materials on teaching data science with AI built into coursework, including a student AGENTS.md that tutors rather than solves.

## Evidence and inquiry: philosophical foundations

- Bergstrom, Carl T. & West, Jevin D. (2020). Calling Bullshit: The Art of Skepticism in a Data-Driven World. *Random House*. [Link](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/563882/calling-bullshit-by-carl-t-bergstrom-and-jevin-d-west/9780525509196/)  
  Practical skepticism about quantitative claims, selection effects, and causal interpretation.
- Dewey, John (1938). Logic: The Theory of Inquiry. *Henry Holt*.  
  Source of 'warranted assertibility': conclusions are justified by the inquiry that supports them.
- Frankfurt, Harry G. (2005). On Bullshit. *Princeton University Press*. [Link](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt7t4wr)  
  Distinguishes indifference to truth from lying; fluent output does not supply warrant (essay first published 1986).
- Haack, Susan (2003). Defending Science—Within Reason: Between Scientism and Cynicism. *Prometheus Books*. [Link](https://repository.law.miami.edu/fac_books/146/)  
  Fallibilist assessment of evidence, between scientism and cynicism.
- Hicks, Michael Townsen; Humphries, James & Slater, Joe (2024). ChatGPT is bullshit. *Ethics and Information Technology* 26: 38. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10676-024-09775-5)  
  Applies Frankfurt to language-model output; a contested philosophical argument, not an error rate.
- Longino, Helen E. (1990). Science as Social Knowledge: Values and Objectivity in Scientific Inquiry. *Princeton University Press*. [Link](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctvx5wbfz)  
  Objectivity through social criticism; an agreeable assistant cannot replace a critical community.
- McIntyre, Lee (2019). The Scientific Attitude: Defending Science from Denial, Fraud, and Pseudoscience. *MIT Press*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/12203.001.0001)  
  Science grounded in caring about evidence and being willing to change one's mind.

## Principles and guidance for responsible use

- Blau, Wolfgang; Cerf, Vinton G.; Enriquez, Juan, et al. (2024). Protecting scientific integrity in an age of generative AI. *PNAS* 121(22): e2407886121. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2407886121)  
  Editorial from an NAS-convened panel: accountability, disclosure, verification, documentation, and oversight.
- Castellacci, F., et al. (2026). Generative artificial intelligence in scientific research: Individual benefits, collective risks, and a framework for responsible research with AI. *arXiv:2607.24879*. [Preprint] [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2607.24879)  
  Framework weighing individual gains against collective risks to science.
- Committee on Publication Ethics (2023). Authorship and AI tools: COPE position statement. . [Link](https://publicationethics.org/cope-position-statements/ai-author)  
  AI tools cannot be authors; authors are responsible for all content and must disclose use.
- European Commission, ERA Forum (2026). Living guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research (third version). *European Commission*. [Link](https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/news/all-research-and-innovation-news/updated-era-living-guidelines-responsible-use-generative-ai-research-2026-05-08_en)  
  Living guidance for researchers, institutions, and funders in the European Research Area.
- Hosseini, M. & Horbach, S. P. J. M. (2023). Fighting reviewer fatigue or amplifying bias? Considerations and recommendations for use of ChatGPT and other large language models in scholarly peer review. *Research Integrity and Peer Review* 8: 4. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-023-00133-5)  
  Peer review as a human, community judgment, and what language models would change about it.
- International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (2026). Recommendations, Section V: Use of artificial intelligence in publishing. . [Link](https://www.icmje.org/recommendations/browse/artificial-intelligence/)  
  Publisher-side expectations for disclosure, placement, and responsibility (updated January 2026).
- Knöchel, T.-D.; Schweizer, K. J.; Acar, O. A., et al. (2025). Core principles of responsible generative AI usage in research. *AI and Ethics* 5: 6371-6377. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00768-8)  
  Consensus principles, including data protection and when documentation of AI use is needed.
- National Institutes of Health (2023). The use of generative artificial intelligence technologies is prohibited for the NIH peer review process (NOT-OD-23-149). *NIH*. [Link](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-23-149.html)  
  Funder prohibition on AI in grant review, grounded in confidentiality.
- National Science Foundation (2023). Notice to research community: Use of generative artificial intelligence technology in the NSF merit review process. *NSF*. [Link](https://www.nsf.gov/news/notice-to-the-research-community-on-ai)  
  Sharing proposal content with AI tools breaches merit-review confidentiality.
- Resnik, David B. & Hosseini, Mohammad (2024). The ethics of using artificial intelligence in scientific research: New guidance needed for a new tool. *AI and Ethics*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-024-00493-8)  
  Accountability, transparency, fairness, and reproducibility as research-ethics questions.
- UNESCO (2021). Recommendation on Open Science. *UNESCO*. [Link](https://www.unesco.org/en/legal-affairs/recommendation-open-science)  
  International instrument making equity, infrastructure, and access integral to open science.
- UNESCO (2023). Guidance for generative AI in education and research. *UNESCO*. [Link](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research)  
  Human-centred guidance on learning, agency, inclusion, and governance.
- van Dis, Eva A. M.; Bollen, Johan; Zuidema, Willem; van Rooij, Robert & Bockting, Claudi L. (2023). ChatGPT: Five priorities for research. *Nature* 614: 224-226. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-023-00288-7)  
  Early agenda for governing language-model use in research.

## Disclosing and documenting AI use

- Cwik, Jan Christopher (2026). Disclosure is not documentation: An open science framework for documenting generative AI use in scholarly research and publication workflows. *Research Integrity and Peer Review* 11: 47. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-026-00245-8)  
  Task-specific documentation with reusable templates; the closest framework to CRASR's ai-use log.
- Hosseini, M.; Gordijn, B.; Kaebnick, G. E. & Holmes, K. (2025). Disclosing generative AI use for writing assistance should be voluntary. *Research Ethics*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1177/17470161251345499)  
  Argues writing assistance need not be disclosed; contrast with mandatory-disclosure positions.
- Hosseini, M.; Resnik, D. B. & Holmes, K. (2023). The ethics of disclosing the use of artificial intelligence tools in writing scholarly manuscripts. *Research Ethics*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1177/17470161231180449)  
  Early ethical case for disclosing AI use in manuscripts.
- Luo, X., et al. (2025). Reporting guideline for the use of generative artificial intelligence tools in medical research: The GAMER statement. *BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjebm-2025-113825)  
  Delphi reporting guideline: tool, purpose, prompts, and verification.
- Resnik, David B. & Hosseini, Mohammad (2025). Disclosing artificial intelligence use in scientific research and publication: When should disclosure be mandatory, optional, or unnecessary?. *Accountability in Research*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1080/08989621.2025.2481949)  
  Ties the need for disclosure to what the AI did, the basis for CRASR's risk tiers.
- STM Association (2025). Recommendations for a classification of AI use in academic manuscript preparation. *STM*. [Link](https://stm-assoc.org/document/recommendations-for-a-classification-of-ai-use-in-academic-manuscript-preparation/)  
  Publisher classification of AI uses and which need disclosure.
- Suchikova, Y.; Tsybuliak, N.; Teixeira da Silva, J. A. & Nazarovets, S. (2025). GAIDeT (Generative AI Delegation Taxonomy): A taxonomy for humans to delegate tasks to generative artificial intelligence in scientific research and publishing. *Accountability in Research*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1080/08989621.2025.2544331)  
  Taxonomy of tasks delegated to AI, with a declaration generator.
- The Scholarly Kitchen (2026). Guest post: Research needs a shared standard for AI disclosure. . [Link](https://scholarlykitchen.sspnet.org/2026/07/13/guest-post-research-needs-a-shared-standard-for-ai-disclosure/)  
  On the World Conferences on Research Integrity effort toward one disclosure standard.
- Wahle, J. P.; Ruas, T.; Mohammad, S. M.; Meuschke, N. & Gipp, B. (2023). AI Usage Cards: Responsibly reporting AI-generated content. *2023 ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries (JCDL)*: 282-284. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1109/JCDL57899.2023.00060)  
  Structured, machine-readable reporting of AI use, including how output was checked.
- Weaver, Kari D. (2024). The Artificial Intelligence Disclosure (AID) Framework: An introduction. *College & Research Libraries News* 85(10): 407-411. [Link](https://doi.org/10.5860/crln.85.10.407)  
  Stage-by-stage disclosure statement format; the source of CRASR's log stages.
- World Bank (2026). Documenting AI use for reproducible research. *World Bank Reproducible Research Repository*. [Link](https://worldbank.github.io/wb-reproducible-research-repository/guidance/AI_reproducibility_guidelines.html)  
  Separates AI as coding help from AI outputs used as data; what to keep for each.

## Scientific workflow, statistics, and reproducibility

- Gelman, Andrew, et al. (2020). Bayesian workflow. *arXiv:2011.01808*. [Preprint] [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2011.01808)  
  Iterative model building, computational and model checking, comparison, and understanding.
- Kapoor, Sayash & Narayanan, Arvind (2023). Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science. *Patterns* 4(9): 100804. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2023.100804)  
  Data leakage across many fields; check validation design before trusting performance.
- Kapoor, Sayash, et al. (2024). REFORMS: Consensus-based recommendations for machine-learning-based science. *Science Advances* 10: eadk3452. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adk3452)  
  Consensus checklist for conducting and reporting ML-based research.
- Nosek, Brian A., et al. (2015). Promoting an open research culture. *Science* 348: 1422-1425. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aab2374)  
  TOP guidelines: graded, implementable transparency standards for journals.
- Shmueli, Galit (2010). To explain or to predict?. *Statistical Science* 25(3): 289-310. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-STS330)  
  Explanatory and predictive goals call for different models and validation; decide which before modeling.
- Smith, G. R.; Bello, C.; Bialic-Murphy, L., et al. (2024). Ten simple rules for using large language models in science, version 1.0. *PLOS Computational Biology* 20(1): e1011767. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011767)  
  Practical rules for researchers using language models.

## AI in ecology and environmental science

- Cooper, Natalie; Clark, Adam T.; Lecomte, Nicolas; Qiao, Huijie & Ellison, Aaron M. (2024). Harnessing large language models for coding, teaching and inclusion to empower research in ecology and evolution. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 15(10): 1757-1763. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14325)  
  Perspective on coding, teaching, and inclusion, with a road map for responsible use.
- Ferrari, Nina C.; Conklin, E. E.; Fitch, A. A., et al. (2026). Thinking outside the black box: Seven guidelines for GenAI use in the ecological sciences. *Ecology and Evolution* 16(8): e74118. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.74118)  
  Seven guidelines tying AI use to ecological theory, expertise, transparency, and equity.
- Johnson, Thomas F.; Simmons, Benno I.; Millard, Joseph; Strydom, Tanya; Danet, Alain; Sweeny, Amy R. & Evans, Luke C. (2024). Pressure to publish introduces large-language model risks. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 15(10): 1771-1773. [Link](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/218025)  
  Response to Cooper et al.: publication pressure turns language-model shortcuts into risks to quality and training.
- King, R. A.; Abowd, L.; Broderick, C. W., et al. (2026). Ten simple rules for effective use of generative AI for code development in environmental science. *PLOS Computational Biology* 22(8): e1014627. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014627)  
  Rules for AI-assisted coding written for environmental scientists.
- Mammides, Christos & Papadopoulos, Harris (2024). The role of large language models in interdisciplinary research: Opportunities, challenges and ways forward. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 15(10): 1774-1776. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14398)  
  Language models as bridges between fields, and the risks for complex tasks.

## AI-generated code: pitfalls and practice

- Ahmad, M. O. (2026). Comprehension debt in GenAI-assisted software engineering projects. *30th International Conference on Evaluation and Assessment in Software Engineering (EASE 2026)*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.13277)  
  Defines comprehension debt: the gap between the code a team has and the code it understands.
- Becker, Joel; Rush, Nate; Barnes, Elizabeth & Rein, David (2025). Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developer productivity. *arXiv:2507.09089*. [Preprint] [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.09089)  
  Randomized trial: experienced developers believed AI sped them up but were 19% slower.
- Fawzy, A.; Tahir, A. & Blincoe, K. (2025). Vibe coding in practice: Motivations, challenges, and a future outlook – a grey literature review. *arXiv:2510.00328*. [Preprint] [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2510.00328)  
  Defines vibe coding and reviews what practitioners report about it.
- He, Hao; Miller, Courtney; Agarwal, Shyam; Kästner, Christian & Vasilescu, Bogdan (2026). Speed at the cost of quality: How Cursor AI increases short-term velocity and long-term complexity in open-source projects. *23rd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR 2026)*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2511.04427)  
  Projects adopting an AI coding agent sped up briefly, then slowed as complexity and warnings rose.
- Liu, Yue; Widyasari, Ratnadira; Irsan, Ivana Clairine; Chen, Junkai, et al. (2026). Debt behind the AI boom: A large-scale empirical study of AI-generated code in the wild. *arXiv:2603.28592*. [Preprint] [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.28592)  
  About 300,000 AI-written commits: the technical debt they introduced, mostly code smells, often persisted.
- Merz, Evan X. (2026). AI usage generates a fragile codebase. . [Blog post] [Link](https://evanxmerz.com/post/ai-usage-generates-a-fragile-codebase/)  
  Practitioner essay on bloated helpers, shallow tests, and skimmed reviews.

## Environmental costs and equity

- Bender, Emily M.; Gebru, Timnit; McMillan-Major, Angelina & Shmitchell, Shmargaret (2021). On the dangers of stochastic parrots: Can language models be too big?. *Proceedings of the 2021 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1145/3442188.3445922)  
  Scale, training data, environmental cost, and unequal harms.
- Houston Advanced Research Center (2026). Thirsty data and the Lone Star State: The impact of data center growth on Texas' water supply. *HARC*. [Link](https://harcresearch.org/news/texas-data-center-boom-could-consume-up-to-161-billion-gallons-of-water-annually-by-2030/)  
  Texas data-center water use now and projected to 2030.
- Li, P.; Yang, J.; Islam, M. A. & Ren, S. (2025). Making AI less 'thirsty': Uncovering and addressing the secret water footprint of AI models. *Communications of the ACM*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2304.03271)  
  Water footprint of AI, counting on-site cooling and electricity generation.
- Luccioni, Sasha; Jernite, Yacine & Strubell, Emma (2024). Power hungry processing: Watts driving the cost of AI deployment?. *Proceedings of the 2024 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1145/3630106.3658542)  
  Measured inference energy across tasks and models.
- Schwartz, Roy; Dodge, Jesse; Smith, Noah A. & Etzioni, Oren (2020). Green AI. *Communications of the ACM* 63(12): 54-63. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1145/3381831)  
  Efficiency as a research goal alongside accuracy.
- Shehabi, A., et al. (2024). 2024 United States data center energy usage report. *Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL-2001637)*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.71468/P1WC7Q)  
  US data centers used 4.4% of electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7-12% by 2028.
- Strubell, Emma; Ganesh, Ananya & McCallum, Andrew (2019). Energy and policy considerations for deep learning in NLP. *Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the ACL*. [Link](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/P19-1355)  
  Foundational estimates of training costs and access barriers; not current per-prompt figures.
